I honestly was not expecting it to be THIS bad. It's almost insulting how stupid and ham-fisted this movie is. Donald Shirley was a real, very interesting person. And he's the most interesting character in this movie. But he's sidelined so that we can watch a oafish bafoon who worked for him one time learn what racism is.

This movie is genuinely so bad. Like insane to think that the thesis to a period piece about racism is a steven universe-esque "Everyone Can Be Kind, You Just Have To Look For It". REALLY victim-blamey overall ??? Generally the whole premise is "What if a white person was an uncivilized savage and a black person was..... smart ??? and clean ???" The director clearly thinks this is subversive, implying that he assumes the opposite to be the default. Obviously this adds a new undertone that what actually makes someone gross and violent is being poor. A couple notable scenes in the movie : - Don is forced by Tony to eat fried chicken. He says "no" at first, repulsed by the idea of adhering to a stereotype, but ends up caving in and enjoying it. This scene is meant to be comedic and heartwarming, mostly at Don's expense, for even daring to refuse fried chicken. - Don and Tony get stopped by a white police officer while getting home, making the former very anxious, due to his past misadventures with racist cops. However, this one is just plain nice, as Not All Cops Are Bastards, wishes them a Merry Christmas and lets them go. In summary, this movie is insanely racist, and makes blatantly false assumptions about racism in the 60s. It treats racism as an individual rather than systemic problem : you are expected to accept racism as an unchangeable truth of the world in order to engage with this piece. I'd give zero stars if I could.

This movie tries so hard to portray some, modern-day white hero shit while quite literally overshadowing the black, gay, genius storyline. Who cares about Tony's inability to speak properly and write to his wife when Doc has such a rich history that was blatantly disregarded or bypassed to get to the rest of the story. Doc literally said “So, if I'm not black enough, and if I'm not white enough, and if I'm not man enough, then tell me, Tony, what am I?” and then they didn’t address it at all. I feel like it didn’t do the movie as a whole proper justice, and it felt like it focused way too much on an Italian white man with a “hard name” to pronounce. I looked it up and saw how much this movie is based on facts, it truly makes much more sense. The script was heavily based on the personal accounts, letters, and audio tapes of the driver, Tony "Lip" Vallelonga. It faced severe backlash from the family of pianist Dr. Don Shirley, who called the movie a "symphony of lies" and a skewed version of reality. So fuck you all.

Reducing racism to one white guy's personal journey from prejudice to friendship is certainly one way to make a deeply systemic issue feel nice and digestible. White guy is racist, black guy suffers, white guy learns some empathy, everyone goes home. Systemic racism has been defeated. Oh and of course they ate fried chicken together. One star because the acting was good.

If I’m not black enough and if I’m not white enough, and not man enough, then tell me Tony, what am I? an absolutely terrible attempt at handling racism. maybe this movie would have worked in the 60s or 70s, but to be made in 2018 is just a complete joke. doesnt do anything to actually tackle social issues. the scene near the end when the cop stops them to tell them their tire was flat is eye-rollingly bad. now that tony has learned racism is bad now the cops in the north are actually good guys here to help them like cmon you cant be serious with this. viggo does a terrible italian accent that feels like a parody of tony soprano and robert de niro, while shoving his face with food in literally every scene. mahershala ali was amazing, its just a shame he was trapped in this movie instead of a good movie. and this movie completely skipped over the queer aspects of dr shirley besides a quick mention of it. cant handle two social issues at the same time, especially when theyre doing such a poor job at the first one and then to top it all off to learn that dr shirleys family didnt want this movie made and heavily over emphasized his friendship with tony that wasnt actually great at all. this movie just feels regressive in so many ways and not the kind of anti racism movie that is going to bring us forward in the modern era. cannot believe this movie won best picture.

On the one hand, yes, the acting is great, you’ve got Viggo Mortensen, who very rarely turns in a bad performance and is very selective when it comes to picking the right script to work on and knowing if he can make something good come out of it which he does here, and Mahershala Ali, what more do I even need to say about him that he hasn’t done already, he’s a fantastic actor and in the years since he gained a bigger spotlight he’s got Curious Case Of Benjamin Button, Predators, Hunger Games: Mockingjay, Moonlight, Hidden Figures, True Detecitve season 3, Spider-Man: Into The Spiderverse, even his channeled Wesley Snipes performance in Alita: Battle Angel was great, this guy is a fantastic actor and rightfully deserved to win Best Supporting Actor this year. If anything these two guys are the reason why the film is salvageable. But other than that, everything else about this movie is just bland and forgettable. For one thing, it’s a bad sign in the family of the person you’re making the movie off of had no idea they were even making the film without them knowing. Yeah, no joke, Shirley’s relatives condemned the film, stating that they were not contacted by studio representatives until after development, and that it misrepresented Shirley’s relationship with his family. Don’s brother Maurice Shirley said, “My brother never considered Tony to be his ‘friend’; he was an employee, his chauffeur (who resented wearing a uniform and cap). This is why context and nuance are so important. The fact that a successful, well-to-do black artist would employ domestics that did NOT look like him, should not be lost in translation.” Mahershala Ali responded with an apology to Shirley’s nephew Edwin Shirley III, saying that “I did the best I could with the material I had” and that he was not aware that there were “close relatives with whom I could have consulted to add some nuance to the character”. Writer-director Peter Farrelly said that he was under the impression that there “weren’t a lot of family members” still alive, that they did not take major liberties with the story, and that relatives of whom he was aware had been invited to a private screening for friends and family. Nick Vallelonga, Vallelonga’s son, acknowledged that members of the Shirley family were hurt that he did not speak to them, and that he was sorry that they were offended. He told Variety that “Don Shirley himself told me not to speak to anyone” and that Shirley “approved what I put in and didn’t put in.” That’s already a bad sign right out of the gate. Another problem the movie has is that follows the white savior stereotype/cliché. Peter Farrelly told Entertainment Weekly that he was aware of the white savior trope before filming and sought to avoid it. He said he had long discussions with the actors and producers on the point, and believes that it was not advanced by the film, saying it is “about two guys who were complete opposites and found a common ground, and it’s not one guy saving the other. It’s both saving each other and pulling each other into some place where they could bond and form a lifetime friendship.” New York Times writer Wesley Morris characterized Green Book as being a “racial reconciliation fantasy”. Morris argues that the film represents a specific style of racial storytelling “in which the wheels of interracial friendship are greased by employment, in which prolonged exposure to the black half of the duo enhances the humanity of his white, frequently racist counterpart”. Writing in The Hollywood Reporter, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar noted that “filmmakers are history’s interpreters, not its chroniclers.” Because when I think of somebody trying to avoid falling into clichés, it’s Peter Farrelly, whose last big directing contribution to the world was the shitpile that was Movie 43….oops. But let’s get down to the real reason why this movie does not work at all, it’s fucking Driving Miss Daisy all over again, just reverse the races, make Jessica Lange Mahershala Ali and make Morgan Freeman Viggo Mortensen and bang, it’s pretty much the same movie, there is nothing clever or unique about this movie. It’s just an Oscar bait film, the same typical Oscar bait film that we’ve been trying to get rid of for years now, and the worst part about all of this is that there was a far superior Oscar bait film that got completely snubbed this year and that was A Star Is Born, that was an example of an Oscar bait movie done 100% right avoiding a lot of the tropes and clichés and creating new twists and turns with it to create not only a great movie but one of the best movies of last year….and it got completely snubbed at the Oscars only winning 1 of its’ 8 nominations while Green Book got 3. While Green Book doesn’t level my complete anger at winning Best Picture for a lackluster movie like The King’s Speech did in 2010, the fact that Green Book won the Best Picture proves that no matter how much the Oscars thinks it’s changing its’ course and getting its’ shit together, they’re still stuck in the past by letting generic shit like this winning the top prize and trying to make people think that this was the definitive movie of the year. Green Book is just an bore of a film, I really tried to give it a fair shot but I’m sorry, this is one of the dullest and blandest Best Picture winners ever, other than Mortensen and Ali, the rest of the movie is just a forgettable lump, it’s just a bore, a bore of a film that doesn’t work at all.

Um filme que fala de um pianista negro bom pra caralho nos anos 60. O filme, de fato, é sobre ele? Não, é sobre o motorista branco racista, que aparentemente deixou de ser racista quando passa o filme inteiro. Adivinha? Sendo racista e passando pano pra racista. O filme tenta até  avançar um pouco a “crítica”, mas recua, e fica um grande poço que não é nada profundo. Apesar de ser uma história real, o filme usa a história do Dr. Shirley apenas como base, para enaltecer o Tony, o grande salvador. Não é à toa que a produção foi também feita pelo filho do próprio. A única coisa boa nesse filme é a atuação do Mahershala Ali, que ganhou o Oscar como ator coadjuvante pelo filme. Sim, o filme não é sobre o personagem dele, o que é bem escroto. Esse filme ter ganhado o Oscar de Melhor Filme é loucura.

He is the perfect foil to Dr. Shirley, who is obnoxious, cerebral, classist, obtuse and naive, but we’ll forgive him all that because he’s a lonely, misunderstood and repressed Negro homosexual. Fun for the whole family! Additional fantasies include: Back to the Future-style impromptu rock and roll scene, gratuitous home-for-Christmas ending, surprising nice cop to contrast with evil cops, and a ringer appearance from the greatest white savior of them all: Bobby Kennedy. Plus not one but two supporting actors from early aughts Disney Channel shows playing Southern racists. And a wide array of Italian racial epithets for Black people! Honestly veeeeery shape of water vibes. #movies

I want to make very clear: this is in no way a defense of an extremely mediocre movie that under no fucking circumstances should have been in the oscar conversation let along won best fucking picture. Some rank, evil shit in this of course, but occasional moments of beauty, as is inevitable in something so relentlessly sentimental. My favorite is when Tony Lip—who has been learning how to be more romantic from Doc Shirley—writes his wife a letter that reads, “You remind me of a house. A beautiful house where all the lights are on and everyone is happy inside.” And goddamnit that is what it’s like to feel in love. Some nice tensions too. Doc Shirley is allowed to be a complicated figure—a drunk, a promiscuous gay man, and at war with the balance between “respectable” white culture and what white people would perceive as the baseness of black culture. Tony Lip is a harder pill to swallow. It is true that there is a type of guy who is so ignorant and vulgar that he feels more harmless than his more ideologically-considered peers, but the movie elides much of the nastiness that still lives in these types. Not quite as bad as I was expecting, but—again—the academy should be drawn and quartered for this one. Boneheads, the lot of them.

Like it's 2 hours and ten minutes of nothing. I will say my biggest complaint is that I just can not buy the characters journey. I don't care about historical accuracy or fully representing the person the movie is based on rather than building a narrative around the idea of a person (though to some extent I do see a difference when the fictionalization would be far less interesting than the real story such as here). I get that. But your fictionalized dramatized version of the characters still have to make since in your world. I don't buy for a second that a man who is in the upper crust of black musical artist doesn't know who Aretha Franklin is. Doesn't know exactly what to expect in the Jim crow south. Maybe he tries making a statement and feigning ignorance, but the character (note I'm saying character) seems to be legitimately caught off guard by racism in the Jim Crow South and I do not buy it for a second. Put this with weird things this movie includes that just adds to its frankly weird approach to 1960s racism, like the scene where Don Shirley discovers fried chicken(?) it just makes the whole thing seem insincere and wild. Not to say there's no attempt at anything in the other direction, but it is so clear this wasn't made with much thought about what the lived experience and perspective of either the real life Don Shirley or fictionalized Don  Shirley would have been. Also those letters were ass

I don't know yes it was heartwarming but this film annoyed me, starting with the fact that it isn't historically accurate; for instance, Shirley’s run-in with the police didn't end in an arrest and actually took place in West Virginia. Shirley wasn't cut off from his family either he stayed in touch with them yet the film portrays him as an isolated man. It also suggests that Shirley was almost completely cut off from Black culture, which wasn't true. It’s a fable about the transformation of a white protagonist. The story’s focus shifts from the issue of racial segregation itself to Tony’s personal growth. *Green Book* simplifies racism by suggesting that the friendship between Shirley and Tony can solve the problem. In reality, however, the issue lies in structural and systemic forms of prejudice. The film also tasks Shirley with rediscovering his "Black identity" in a very stereotypical way - eating KFC, listening to specific music. You can detect a hint of paternalism here; Tony acts as a mentor guiding Shirley toward this stereotypical Black identity. I see a depiction of events that reflects a liberal perspective... It’s a romanticized fantasy of reconciliation that masks structural racial inequality. Two scenes involving police officers stuck with me: one in the South, where Shirley was supposedly arrested, and one in the North, where an officer let them go. The North represented by the polite officer becomes a symbol of "progressive America," ignoring the fact that such problems were very much present in the North as well. It’s a typical liberal narrative. The *Green Book* itself was necessary even in the North. Schools there were still segregated, workplace discrimination existed, and Black people couldn't rent apartments in certain neighborhoods. So, *Green Book* is essentially a liberal fairy tale about reconciliation that reduces the problem of racism to individual transformation. Shirley is reduced to a figure whom Tony must understand and WTF -teach how to discover his Black identity. It also allows the viewer to believe that the problem lies only with the South, rather than with America and the entire system itself. Racism-historically rooted in slavery, class, labor, and capitalism-is flattened, and the film delivers a "white savior" narrative.

I get why people said this was boring, I stopped at the halfway point for about a month. I’m a sucker for some wholesome interactions, there were enough sweet scenes between the two trying to understand one another that made me want to finish the whole thing. However, everything else is just very bland. It doesn’t really take any steps to make a well defined stance on anything and even trips over itself in the process. Like in the beginning it shows that Tony’s got some racism in him but at the end, he’s lecturing Dr. Shirley about how he lives among minorities and understands them better because he’s not all pompous like him. Feels like he should’ve started off jumping to the defense from the get-go because of that more personal background. Also they can’t really make up their mind on what’s worth pushing back on. They have multiple run-ins with racist cops, establishments, and just general people but it feels like Tony can’t make up his mind on how much injustice to let slide before doing something about it. I thought the idea behind Dr. Shirley being caught between two worlds was very interesting but that doesn’t get given the time I think it really deserved.

The whole white savior narrative really ruined it for me. It felt like the movie was more interested in making Tony the hero who learns to overcome racism than actually centering Don Shirley’s experience Almost making America look like the savior…

The idea that “we should love one another because it’s Christmas” isn’t a message. It really could have been a truly important, truly meaningful film, but in the end, they didn’t want to make it that way. I really regret that. It’s a clichéd, boring story—despite its theme and surface, it’s a colorful, lively comedy that seems to be downright afraid to delve deeper into a social problem that is indeed important and still very much present today, and for that very reason, it’s an experience you can safely skip. If you’re interested in the topic of racism, I can wholeheartedly recommend the film *The Hate U Give*, which, - although it doesn't delve nearly as deeply into the subject as it should - conveys a much richer and more thought-provoking message.

Something about this movie was off. Like idk what it was, or if im too WOKE, but this just felt off. Don’t get me wrong, I love Viggo Mortensen and Mahershala Ali (they’re both so extremely elegant in their own ways). Maybe it’s just these kinds of movies that sorta hit me weird. I thought it would be more about the civil rights movement, but it’s more about italian guy being rude and taking too long to learn manners. Ali’s performance was great, and he delivered my favorite quote from this movie beautifully: “If im not black enough, if im not white enough, and if im not man enough, then what am I?”

This movie’s commentary on blackness is thinner than a piece of paper, and its understanding of racism in America is incredibly cartoonish. That said, Mahershala Ali takes this surface-level material about racial and sexual identity and attempts to translate it with some nuance. Viggo Mortensen is also quite funny. Other than that, the dialogue is laughable and I really dislike the score. Visually, it’s fine. I liked the piano playing. It’s occasionally wholesome, but its charming nature is more or less stamped by its excessive sentimentality. As a whole, whatever.

Insane on a multitude of levels that something this dated and clueless was not only released in 2018, but also won best picture the following February (well, maybe that isn't so surprising). Green Book is constantly trying to stir it's audience with it's glib angle that "the black guy is a virtuosic and cultured intellect and the white guy is a blue collar schlub who is in a sense closer to black culture than he is" but that can only work if you maintain the very same narrow and old-fashioned view of blackness it purports to wag it's finger at while simultaneously playing to and culturing in it's audience. I have to wonder what person born after 1980 could take this self-satisfied "heartwarming" white savior shit seriously on any level.
